l: honor and noble reputation, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. This land is ever willing to aid in a just cause those in difficulty;
s: Macaria chooses death because she considers it more honorable than surviving as a coward or being abandoned after the fall of the city. She asks to be remembered and buried honorably, and the Chorus declares that her virtue will win a glorious reputation among men.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: The Chorus invokes the earth, moon, divine rays, and Minerva for news and protection. The speaker says that, for the sake of the country and house, the speaker has received suppliants and is prepared to face danger rather than surrender them to Argos. Mycenae is described as a prosperous and warlike city that secretly resents the speaker's land. The speaker calls on Minerva and Jupiter to defend the land and prevent the hostile force from Argos from driving the speaker away.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: The Chorus calls on the earth, moon, divine rays, and Minerva to bring news and announce the speaker's situation in heaven and at Minerva's throne.

l: Minerva, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: Minerva is invoked as the blue-eyed queen and as the goddess whose soil and city are under her care. The speaker asks her to lead away by another path the person who unjustly brings the spear-brandishing host from Argos.

l: the land of Erectheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: The speaker acts on behalf of the country and refuses to surrender strangers at the bidding of Argos. The country is described as facing secret anger from Mycenae.

l: the Heraclids, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: The speaker has received the suppliants and is prepared to cut through danger on behalf of them, the speaker's country, and the speaker's house.

l: Mycenae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: Mycenae is described as a prosperous city, highly praised for valor in war, that secretly harbors anger against the speaker's land.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: Argos demands that the strangers be given up. Its forces are described as a spear-brandishing host threatening the speaker's position.

l: the host from Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: The host from Argos is being unjustly led against the speaker's land. The speaker asks Minerva to divert the person leading it.

l: Jove, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: Jupiter is called the speaker's ally, and the speaker trusts that Jupiter rightly favors the speaker. The speaker believes the gods will not appear inferior to men.

l: Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. O earth, and moon that shinest through the night, and most brilliant
s: The city is presented as the soil and city of Minerva, who is its mother, mistress, and guardian. Its worship includes sacrifices, monthly observances, songs of youths, dances, and nighttime celebrations by virgins on a lofty hill.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: A servant reports to Alcmena that the Athenians and the descendants of Hercules have defeated the Argives, while Iolaus has been rejuvenated and has captured Eurystheus. Eurystheus is brought before Alcmena, who demands his death despite the Athenian law against executing enemies captured alive. Eurystheus reveals Apollo's prophecy that his tomb near the temple of the divine virgin of Pallene will protect Athens and harm its descendants' enemies. Alcmena orders the servants to kill him and give his body to his friends, while the Chorus approves her decision.

l: Alcmena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Alcmena rejoices at the victory and at the survival of Iolaus and the descendants of Hercules. She confronts Eurystheus, condemns his treatment of Hercules, herself, and their children, and insists on killing him despite the city's law. She orders the servants to kill Eurystheus and give his body to the dogs.

l: Servant, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The servant brings Alcmena news of the victory and reports that Iolaus has become young again and captured Eurystheus. He reminds Alcmena that she promised to make him free for bringing the news.

l: Messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The messenger brings Eurystheus before Alcmena after Hyllus and Iolaus have defeated the Argive forces. He explains that Athenian authorities forbid the execution of an enemy captured alive and warns that Alcmena will incur blame if she kills Eurystheus.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The Chorus celebrates the end of fear, the victory of the friends of Alcmena, and the apparent justice of divine action. It advises Alcmena to release Eurystheus because the city has decided that he must not be killed, but later accepts her order against him.

l: Iolaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Iolaus performs glorious deeds in battle despite his age. After praying to Juno and Jupiter, he becomes young for one day, takes Eurystheus's chariot at the Scironian rocks, binds him, and brings him to Alcmena.

l: Hyllus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Hyllus challenges the Argive general to single combat and then returns to his ranks when the challenge is not accepted. He fights in the battle, helps defeat the Argives, and joins Iolaus in setting up a statue of Jupiter in honor of the victory.

l: Eurystheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Eurystheus is captured alive and brought before Alcmena. He defends his actions as compelled by Juno and argues that Athens cannot execute him without violating the laws of the Greeks. He reveals an oracle concerning his future tomb and predicts that, after his death, he will protect Athens and harm its descendants' enemies. Alcmena nevertheless orders his execution.

l: Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Hercules is described as a powerful and worthy man whom Eurystheus feared and persecuted. The Chorus says that Hercules has gone to heaven, his body consumed in fire, and that he now shares the bed of Hebe.

l: Athenians, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The Athenians defend the land that produced and raised them and fight against the Argive army. Their leaders also uphold the rule that an enemy captured alive must not be executed.

l: Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The Argives fight against Athens and the descendants of Hercules under Eurystheus's leadership. Their forces initially break the opposing spear line but are eventually driven into flight.

l: descendants of Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The descendants of Hercules fight with the Athenians and are freed from Eurystheus after the victory. Alcmena tells them that they will return to their father's city, possess their inherited land, and sacrifice to their ancestral gods.

l: Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Athens defeats the force sent against it and protects the descendants of Hercules. Its leaders refuse to execute Eurystheus because he was captured alive, and Eurystheus's prophecy promises that his burial near Athens will protect the city from future attackers.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Argos is represented in the battle by Eurystheus and his army. Eurystheus urges his allies not to disgrace Argos and Mycenae, but the Argive force is defeated.

l: Mycenae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Mycenae is the place from which Eurystheus goes out with his spearmen to attack Athens. Its forces are defeated, and Eurystheus is captured.

l: the battle between Athens and Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The battle begins after a rejected proposal for single combat between Hyllus and the opposing general. The armies clash with spears and chariots; after a difficult fight, the Athenians and the descendants of Hercules put the Argive force to flight.

l: victory over the Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The victory frees the descendants of Hercules from Eurystheus's power. Hyllus and Iolaus honor the victory by setting up a statue of Jupiter, the putter to flight.

l: Iolaus's rejuvenation, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Iolaus prays to Juno and Jupiter to become young for one day and take vengeance on his enemies. Two stars and a dim cloud conceal the chariot, and he emerges with the appearance and arms of a young man.

l: capture of Eurystheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Iolaus seizes Eurystheus's four-horse chariot at the Scironian rocks and binds Eurystheus in fetters. Eurystheus is then brought alive before Alcmena.

l: death of Eurystheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Alcmena declares that Eurystheus must die for his many wrongs and orders the servants to kill him. His death is ordered at the end of the unit, but the text does not narrate its completion.

l: prophecy concerning Eurystheus's tomb, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Eurystheus says that Apollo has ordained that he be buried near the temple of the divine virgin of Pallene. From beneath the earth, he will protect Athens while becoming hostile to the descendants of those who attack the city.

l: Athenian law against executing captured enemies, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The leaders of Athens hold that an enemy captured alive must not be put to death. Eurystheus says that killing him would bring pollution under the laws of the Greeks, and the messenger says that the city has released him for this reason.

l: divine justice and fortune, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: The servant says that Eurystheus's reversal of fortune shows that mortals should not envy anyone who appears prosperous until that person is dead. The Chorus presents the victory as evidence that the gods humble the arrogance of the unjust and bring unexpected good fortune.

l: Eurystheus's tomb, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERV. O mistress, I bring news most concise for you to hear, and to myself
s: Eurystheus's tomb is to be located near the temple of the divine virgin of Pallene. He says that the tomb will benefit Athens and harm the descendants of its future enemies, and he forbids libations and blood offerings there.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The unit consists of notes on the Heraclidae, especially their exile, military arrangements, religious observances, and related tragic passages. It discusses Macaria's voluntary sacrifice after an oracle required that a descendant of Hercules be devoted. The notes also compare passages from Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, and other authors, while addressing disputed readings, emendations, and grammatical constructions.

l: The Heraclidae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes concern the Heraclidae and annotate passages involving their condition, movements, military preparations, religious practices, and defense.

l: descendants of Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The Heraclidae are discussed in connection with exile, the arrangement of battle, and the requirement that one of Hercules's descendants be devoted.

l: Macaria, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Macaria, the daughter of Hercules by Deianira, voluntarily offered herself for sacrifice after the oracle required one of Hercules's descendants to be devoted. Her name was afterward given to a fountain.

l: oracle, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The oracle expressly required that one of the descendants of Hercules should be devoted.

l: the prophecy requiring a noble virgin's sacrifice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The sacrifice involved Macaria's voluntary offering of herself in response to the oracle. The notes state that Euripides omitted the oracle's requirement in order to place Macaria's noble-mindedness in a stronger light.

l: Greek grammar and textual criticism, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes examine Greek constructions, supplied words, cognate accusatives, and alternative interpretations. They propose or adopt several emendations, question certain readings, identify awkward constructions, and report that Dindorf considered some lines spurious.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Agamemnon tells the Old Man that Calchas has declared that Iphigenia must be sacrificed to Diana so that the Greeks can sail to Troy, but he has changed his mind and writes to Clytaemnestra ordering her not to send their daughter to Aulis. Menelaus intercepts the letter and accuses Agamemnon of abandoning Greece after previously arranging Iphigenia’s supposed marriage to Achilles as a pretext for bringing her to the army. Agamemnon defends his decision by insisting that he will not kill his daughter for Menelaus’s sake or to recover Helen. The brothers quarrel over leadership, popular opinion, loyalty, and Menelaus’s demand that Agamemnon support the expedition against Troy.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Agamemnon reveals that Calchas has ordered the sacrifice of Iphigenia to Diana so that the Greeks may sail to Troy, but he has repented and is sending a letter to prevent Clytaemnestra from bringing her. He argues with Menelaus that he will not kill his daughter to repair Menelaus’s marriage or serve the expedition.

l: old man (in Iphigenia in Aulis), The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: The Old Man serves Agamemnon and is described as faithful to Agamemnon’s wife and household. He is instructed to carry Agamemnon’s sealed letter to Argos, but Menelaus intercepts him, seizes the letter, and threatens him.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Menelaus intercepts Agamemnon’s letter and confronts him for changing his decision about sacrificing Iphigenia. He insists that Agamemnon must honor the Greek cause and reproaches him for altering his conduct after gaining leadership.

l: Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Iphigenia is Agamemnon’s daughter and the person Calchas declares must be sacrificed to Diana for the Greeks to sail. Agamemnon had summoned her under the pretext that she would marry Achilles, but he now seeks to prevent her arrival.

l: Clytemnestra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Clytaemnestra is Agamemnon’s wife and Iphigenia’s mother. Agamemnon’s letter instructs her not to send Iphigenia to Aulis and to postpone the supposed marriage.

l: Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Achilles is presented as the supposed bridegroom in Agamemnon’s deception, although he does not know about the proposed marriage or the plan involving Iphigenia. The chorus describes him as swift in arms and as the son of Thetis, trained by Chiron.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Helen is the daughter of Tyndarus and the wife whom Menelaus seeks to recover. Paris carried her away from Lacedæmon, and her removal led Menelaus to invoke the oath sworn by her suitors and bring the Greeks against Troy.

l: Calchas, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Calchas declares that the Greeks will obtain a voyage and sack Troy only if Iphigenia is sacrificed to Diana. He is one of the few people who knows the truth about Agamemnon’s supposed marriage arrangement for Iphigenia.

l: Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Diana is the goddess to whom Calchas requires Iphigenia to be sacrificed. She is associated with the place at Aulis, where the chorus passes through a wooded area containing many sacrifices.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: The Greeks assemble at Aulis with ships, shields, horses, and chariots to pursue Helen’s recovery and attack Troy. They are unable to sail because of the calm, and Calchas declares that Iphigenia’s sacrifice is required to secure their voyage.

l: Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Aulis is the place where the Greek army and fleet are assembled but detained by a lack of wind. Its Euripus is described as silent and calm, and its narrow straits contain the ships gathered for the expedition.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Troy is the city toward which the Greeks intend to sail and which they plan to sack. The expedition arises from Paris’s removal of Helen and Menelaus’s appeal to the oath of Helen’s former suitors.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Greece is portrayed as seeking vengeance against those who took Helen and as preparing a major undertaking against the barbarians. Menelaus claims that Greece will be humiliated if Agamemnon prevents the army from acting.

l: the Greek expedition against Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: The expedition against Troy is organized by the Greeks after Menelaus invokes the oath sworn by Helen’s suitors. Agamemnon is chosen as its general, but the army remains at Aulis because it lacks a favorable breeze.

l: Iphigenia’s sacrifice at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Calchas declares that the sacrifice of Iphigenia to Diana is necessary for the Greeks to obtain a voyage and sack Troy. Agamemnon first agrees and summons Iphigenia through a false marriage proposal, then changes his mind and attempts to cancel the sacrifice.

l: Iphigenia's supposed marriage to Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Agamemnon invents a marriage between Iphigenia and Achilles to persuade Clytaemnestra to send their daughter to Aulis. Achilles is unaware that the marriage is only a pretext and does not know what Agamemnon and the other informed leaders are planning.

l: fall of Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: The Greeks intend to attack and sack Troy after Paris carries Helen away. Calchas tells Agamemnon that the sack will occur only if Iphigenia is sacrificed to Diana.

l: calm at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: A calm prevents the Greeks from sailing from Aulis. The silence of the winds and sea is observed at night, and the army demands that the ships either be dismissed or continue seeking a way to depart.

l: Agamemnon's letter, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Agamemnon’s letter first summoned Iphigenia to Aulis as though she were to marry Achilles, but he writes a new letter ordering Clytaemnestra not to send her and to postpone the marriage. Menelaus breaks the seal and uses the letter to confront Agamemnon.

l: ships, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: The Greek ships gather at Aulis in large numbers, carrying the armies of many Greek leaders. They cannot depart because the winds are calm, and their departure is linked by Calchas to the sacrifice of Iphigenia.

l: leadership and popular opinion, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Agamemnon says that honor and popular opinion are uncertain burdens for leaders. Menelaus accuses him of seeking popularity before becoming leader and then becoming difficult to approach after gaining command of the Greek army.

l: friendship and loyalty, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: The dispute between Agamemnon and Menelaus centers on whether a friend and brother must suffer and act for another’s cause. Agamemnon values loyalty to his household and children, while Menelaus demands loyalty to the Greek expedition and the oath sworn to Tyndarus.

l: marriage and infidelity, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPHIGENIA IN AULIS.
s: Helen’s departure with Paris is treated as the cause of the Greek expedition against Troy. Agamemnon condemns Menelaus for seeking to recover a wife he had failed to govern well, while Menelaus relies on the oath made by Helen’s suitors.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: A Messenger announces that Clytaemnestra, Iphigenia, and Orestes have arrived at Aulis, believing Iphigenia is to marry Achilles. Agamemnon struggles with the necessity of sacrificing his daughter to secure the Greek expedition, while Menelaus reverses his earlier demand and urges him not to kill her. Clytaemnestra questions Agamemnon about the wedding and refuses to return to Argos, while Iphigenia joyfully greets her father without knowing his plan. The Chorus describes Paris and Helen's union, the coming Greek attack on Troy, and the suffering that will follow.

l: Messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: The Messenger announces to Agamemnon that Clytaemnestra, Iphigenia, and Orestes have arrived. He reports that the Greek army is gathering to see Iphigenia and assumes that her arrival concerns a marriage or initiation in honor of Artemis.

l: Agamemnon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Agamemnon is torn between his love for Iphigenia and the pressure to sacrifice her for the Greek expedition. He fears the army, Calchas's prophecy, and the consequences of refusing, and he tries to send Clytaemnestra away before she learns the truth.

l: Clytemnestra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Clytaemnestra arrives with Iphigenia and Orestes, bringing dower-gifts for what she believes is Iphigenia's wedding. She questions Agamemnon about Achilles and the wedding arrangements, then refuses his request that she return to Argos.

l: Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Iphigenia arrives at Aulis believing that she is to marry Achilles. She greets Agamemnon joyfully and speaks of accompanying him, unaware that he intends to offer her in sacrifice.

l: Menelaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Menelaus initially supports Agamemnon but changes his mind after seeing his brother's grief. He tells Agamemnon not to sacrifice Iphigenia and says that the Greek army should be dismissed from Aulis.

l: Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Achilles is presented to Clytaemnestra as the bridegroom promised to Iphigenia. He is described as the son of Peleus and the daughter of Nereus, trained by Chiron and associated with Phthia.

l: Helen, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Helen is described as the cause of the conflict because Paris took her to Greece. The Chorus says that she will later lament after leaving her husband and that her union brings suffering to Greece and Troy.

l: Paris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Paris is described as having been raised as a shepherd at Ida before judging the Goddesses. His union with Helen brings Paris and the Greeks into conflict and leads to the expedition against Troy.

l: Calchas, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Calchas has pronounced a prophecy requiring Iphigenia's sacrifice. Agamemnon fears that Calchas will reveal the prophecy to the Greek army, and he says he will consult Calchas about the Goddess's will.

l: Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Artemis is identified as the Goddess for whom Iphigenia is to be sacrificed. The Messenger also reports that some believe Iphigenia has come to be initiated in Artemis's honor.

l: Greeks, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: The Greeks are assembled at Aulis and prepare to sail against Troy. Their army is said to be capable of forcing Agamemnon to sacrifice Iphigenia and of ravaging Argos if he refuses.

l: Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Aulis is the place where the Greek army is gathered, where Iphigenia arrives, and where Agamemnon plans the sacrifice. The army is expected to sail from Aulis toward Troy.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Argos is the home to which Agamemnon wants Clytaemnestra to return. Agamemnon fears that if he flees there, the Greeks will ravage and destroy the land.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Greece is being drawn into war against Troy because of Paris and Helen. The Chorus describes the Greek army's preparations and the suffering that the conflict will bring.

l: Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Troy is the destination of the Greek expedition and the city against which the Greeks will fight. The Chorus foretells that Troy will be surrounded, ravaged, and made to produce mourning among its women.

l: Hades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Hades is presented as the destination that will quickly attend Iphigenia's supposed nuptials. Agamemnon understands that her wedding is actually connected with her death.

l: altar, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Iphigenia is told that she will stand around the altar during the sacrifice. Agamemnon says that the sacrifice is being prepared at Aulis.

l: Iphigenia’s sacrifice at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: The sacrifice of Iphigenia is demanded by the prophecy and is intended to secure the Greek expedition. Agamemnon feels compelled to carry it out despite his grief, while Menelaus urges him to abandon it.

l: Iphigenia's supposed marriage to Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Iphigenia's wedding is presented publicly as a marriage to Achilles, and Clytaemnestra brings dower-gifts and asks about the ceremony. In reality, Agamemnon connects the supposed wedding with Iphigenia's sacrifice and death.

l: the Trojan War, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: The Trojan War is represented as the conflict between the Greeks and Troy arising from Paris and Helen. The Chorus foretells battles, the destruction of Troy, and mourning among the Trojans.

l: prophecy concerning Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: The prophecy concerning Iphigenia requires her sacrifice for the Greek army's purposes. Agamemnon fears that Calchas will announce it to the army and expose Agamemnon's promise to offer her.

l: Paris and Helen's union, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: Paris and Helen's union is blamed for bringing the Greeks against Troy. The Chorus portrays Paris's desire for Helen and the resulting war as the source of extensive suffering.

l: the Greek expedition against Troy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter a Messenger_.[29]]
s: The army’s expedition to Troy is delayed at Aulis and is connected with the sacrifice demanded from Agamemnon. The Chorus describes the Greeks sailing with ships, arms, shields, and spears to attack Troy.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter_ ACHILLES.]
s: Achilles meets Clytæmnestra and learns from the Old Man that Agamemnon has deceived her by presenting Iphigenia’s journey as a marriage to Achilles. The Greek army intends to sacrifice Iphigenia to Diana so that the expedition can sail to Troy and Menelaus can recover Helen. Achilles promises to oppose the sacrifice and urges Clytæmnestra first to persuade Agamemnon by words. The chorus recalls the wedding of Peleus and Thetis and contrasts it with the fatal marriage-like preparation of Iphigenia.

l: Achilles, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, [_Enter_ ACHILLES.]
s: Achilles waits by the Euripus with the Myrmidons and complains that the Greek expedition is delayed. After learning that Iphigenia has been brought under the pretext of marrying him, he condemns Agamemnon's deception and promises that Iphigenia will not be sacrificed on account of his name or supposed marriage.
